toc.title: So can affirmations change your state?

blocks.p: You might be using positive affirmations as part of your trauma recovery process, or as part of your daily grounding practice. That's fine. But they also might not be helping at all. To understand why, we need to look at how our thoughts are a reflection of the state our body is in, and also how our thoughts affect our body's state.

The words in our brain, and not just the words but the images, the memories, anything happening in our brain that we're aware of: we call those stories. And they follow the state we're in. They're triggered by it.

Here's a small example. I was on a video call with some of my students, and I looked away for a second. I heard a loud noise, looked back, and one of my students was gone from the screen. She was fine. She just needed to plug in. But in that little moment, I noticed a little bit of heat in my body. Not dysregulation exactly, but an ever so slight drop down, probably into flight, more anxious than not.
And the story that popped into my mind was, "Are you okay?" along with an image of her toppling over. Something bad happened.

That's what the brain does. It tries to explain why I'm feeling this way. It tries to create a reference point, like, what can we do about this? So I feel this activation, a very slight amount of mobilization in my system, and my brain says, "This is what happened." There's nothing I can really do about it except say, "Hey, are you okay?" So it gives me an image, and also a potential solution: reach out and ask.

That's the idea of story follows state. We don't even have to have a state shift. We're in a state, and our thoughts follow that state. The thoughts in your brain right now, the images and whatnot, are a direct result of the state you're in right now, in this moment, whether you shift or not.
Deb Dana put it simply when she was on the podcast:

q: You can see how the story changes dependent on the state, not depending on what I choose to think.
blocks.cite: Deb Dana, [Deb Dana Interview: Story Follows State, Climbing the Ladder and Diagnosing (episode 29)](https://player.captivate.fm/episode/f8b9643c-28f8-4185-9525-8b4e6301516c)

blocks.h: So can affirmations change your state?

blocks.p: One student asked the natural next question: if an affirmation repeated over and over can influence your state, how does that fit with story follows state?

Yes, they can. But a couple of students had mixed feelings about them. One said she has a difficult relationship with affirmations because some are too cheesy and drive her crazy. Another said they feel like mind manipulation. The first student said she uses them more as reminders: "Mine tend to be more like, 'You can do hard things,' or, 'You're loved.' They're very general. I'm not trying to manifest anything. I can do hard things. I know I can. I have before, and I continue to do them. So it's more reminding myself."
I think that's a really good point, and I agree. Here's how I'd connect it to story follows state.

The thoughts that naturally occur in our brain follow the state we're in. When I tell you to say something to feel better, that's a thought from my brain and my state. So it's hard for you to take it, embrace it as your own, and use it. It's not your thought. It doesn't come from your state. They're not your words. They're mine.

This connects to something a student brought up with me once: that I was talking from a very safety state place when I said we're always our true self, no matter where we're at. The thoughts I have from my states, if I try to hand them to you and say, "Hey, do this," might be in misalignment with where you're at.
Story follows state, but the flavor of the story also follows your state.

From your safety state, you can say things like, "I love myself," and, "I am so curious about what my internal world is like." From your fight state, you can say, "I love myself," but I don't know if it'll feel the same way. It might feel like, "I love myself more than you, you asshole."
The words might be very similar, but the flavor is going to be different, depending on your state. None of which you choose.

So if I tell you, "Just say this. Count from ten down to one. Tell yourself you're wonderful," that might be in complete misalignment with you, because I might be in my safety state, and my flavor might be, "Oh, the world is beautiful."

The image in my brain is someone white-knuckling the edge of their sink. They're looking in the mirror, tears in their eyes, desperately saying, "You're wonderful. You can do this. You got this." But it's not in alignment. It's not in tune.
To me, that's not helpful. To put it bluntly, that's crazy-making. That's not your thought, and I don't think you're going to get yourself to believe it, especially in a crisis moment like that.
I think affirmations are helpful when you're already grounded in your safety state, and you want to marinate in it, experience it, and build on it. That's wonderful. That's great.

The student who uses them as reminders put it this way: that makes them more of a body safety anchor. If it's something she came up with herself, something that works for her, she can pull it out when she needs it.

Yes. If there's a thought you know will bring up those safety feelings, that's your thought. If you're anchored enough to recall it, and then feel it, you can anchor yourself further. But you obviously have to be anchored enough to have the thought in the first place.

blocks.why: This article talks about anchoring in safety. This practice does just that, tuned to you.

blocks.p: I have one. I have a memory of playing Little League when I was 12. When I want to use my memory or my cognitions to anchor, I can summon that thought, and I can feel that sense of curiosity and wonder and play. That's mine. That's my thought.

Telling me to count from ten down to one is not going to help me. Telling me to imagine a beam of light entering my body, and how beautiful it is, and how connected I am with the world, does not work for me. That's not my thought. I don't think that way. I don't see things that way. It makes no sense to me.
But Little League when I was 12? That was the best. Instantly.

Same with a friend of mine. He'll say, "Hey, remember in high school when we'd play video games and just be nerds all night?" That's the best. Heck yeah, I do. So even if I'm dysregulated, he can say, "Hey, remember that night when..." and it helps, because it's mine. It's in my brain already. It's aligned with something that's safe.
